grammar.example: mi hermano, tus padres, su hija
grammar.en: Possessives before the noun agree in number only: mi hermano, mis hermanos. «Su» = his, her, your (usted) or their.
«Nuestro» (our) also agrees in gender: nuestra madre, nuestros abuelos.
«Tener» (to have) is irregular: tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tienen.

grammar.example: Mi hermana trabaja en un banco.
grammar.en: Regular -ar verbs: hablo, hablas, habla, hablamos, hablan.

grammar.example: mis hermanos = my brothers / my siblings
grammar.en: The masculine plural covers mixed groups: «los padres» = parents, «los hermanos» = siblings.

tips.en: Most Spanish speakers have two last names: the father's first and then the mother's. Emily García López → García is from her dad, López from her mom.
«Mamá» and «papá» are very common even among adults. In Mexico «mami» and «papi» are also used affectionately.
«Parientes» means relatives, not parents. Parents are «los padres».
Family is central in Latin American culture: Sunday lunch with grandparents, aunts and cousins is a classic.
In Spain «vuestro» is «your» for a group (vosotros). In Latin America it's «su»: «su casa» can mean your (plural) house.

story.title: La comida del domingo
story.text: El domingo, la señora Carmen invita a Emily a comer con su familia. En la mesa hay muchas personas. Carmen presenta a todos: «Este es mi esposo, Raúl. Ella es mi hija Lupita, la mamá de Mateo, y él es su esposo, Andrés. Y estos son mis sobrinos, Toño y Paola.» Mateo, el nieto, se sienta al lado de Emily. «¿Tienes hermanos?», pregunta. «Sí, tengo un hermano menor. Se llama Kevin y vive en Chicago con mis padres.» «¿Y abuelos?» «Mi abuela tiene noventa años y todavía cocina muy rico.» Todos ríen. Después de la comida, Raúl saca la guitarra y la familia canta. Emily piensa en su familia y sonríe.
story.en: On Sunday, Mrs. Carmen invites Emily to have lunch with her family. There are lots of people at the table. Carmen introduces everyone: «This is my husband, Raúl. She is my daughter Lupita, Mateo's mom, and he is her husband, Andrés. And these are my nephew and niece, Toño and Paola.» Mateo, the grandson, sits next to Emily. «Do you have siblings?» he asks. «Yes, I have a younger brother. His name is Kevin and he lives in Chicago with my parents.» «And grandparents?» «My grandma is ninety and she still cooks really well.» Everyone laughs. After lunch, Raúl takes out the guitar and the family sings. Emily thinks of her family and smiles.
